jurisdiction.name: Israel
jurisdiction.overview: Israel governs AI through a sectoral, soft-law 'responsible innovation' approach with no AI-specific statute; national AI strategy is now led from the Prime Minister's Office.

narrative.summary: Israel has no AI-specific law. Its 2023 Principles of Policy, Regulation and Ethics in AI, issued by the Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology and the Ministry of Justice, set a 'responsible innovation' model: each regulator acts in its own sector with soft, risk-based tools aligned to international standards, guided by national AI ethics principles. Strategy moved from the TELEM-designed National AI Program (Government Resolution 212 of 2021) to a National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office. The Directorate was set up after the 2025 Nagel Committee report and published the August 2026 National AI Strategic Plan under Government Resolution 4255. Binding obligations come mainly from the Privacy Protection Law, strengthened by Amendment 13 (in force August 2025). The Privacy Protection Authority has issued a draft guideline on applying that law to AI (2025) and guidance on AI agents (2026). Sector regulators are the most active layer: the Bank of Israel's Directive 369 brings AI models under model-risk rules, an inter-ministerial team issued a final report on AI in finance (December 2025), the Ministry of Education regulates generative AI in schools, and the Innovation Authority and Ministry of Health run an AI health sandbox. Inside government, the National Digital Agency's guide on responsible AI use (version 1.0, May 2026) sets risk-tiered approval tracks for public bodies.
lead_institutions: National Artificial Intelligence Directorate, Prime Minister's Office
Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology (MOST)
Ministry of Justice – Office of Legal Counsel and Legislative Affairs
Bank of Israel – Banking Supervision Department
narrative.review_notes: Deep review 2026-10-06. The existing record with title '-' was fixed in place as the December 2023 MOST/MoJ policy principles (id kept). gov.il BlobFolder PDFs could be downloaded with a browser user-agent and were read; gov.il HTML pages (government resolutions, press pages), innovationisrael.org.il (curl), boi.org.il HTML, coe.int and fs.knesset.gov.il (Knesset bills and Reshumot) returned Cloudflare/403 or challenge pages to automated reading. Government Resolutions 3375 (2025), 4255 (2026), 3574 (2025) and 173 (2023) are held as leads because their gov.il pages could not be read or their URLs confirmed. Not recorded: the Israel Bar Association ethics opinion on AI (professional body, not government), the 2022 Tel Aviv University study for the MoJ (academic), Knesset Research and Information Center papers (research, not policy), and the State Comptroller's 2026 parallel audit (to add on a later pass). Standards: the Standards Institution of Israel offers ISO/IEC 42001 certification but no Israeli standard adopting ISO/IEC 42001 or 5339 was found. Procurement: no AI-specific procurement rules found. Cyber: no INCD AI document with an official full text was located (advisory held as a lead). International: Israel signed the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS 225); this is held in data/regional/COE.json, and the PPA draft guidance (April 2025) states that Israel signed it. Unitary state: no subnational pass needed, and no official municipal AI instruments were found.

instruments.current_status: Published final version dated 14 December 2023 (2 Tevet 5784), following the October 2022 public consultation draft. Not adopted by government resolution on the face of the document.
instruments.summary: Final government policy paper (124 pp.) setting Israel's 'responsible innovation' approach: AI regulation should be sectoral rather than horizontal, soft and incremental, risk-based and aligned with emerging international standards. It sets out national AI ethics principles (human-centricity, equality and non-discrimination, transparency and explainability, reliability, safety and security, accountability, privacy) and recommends a government AI knowledge-and-coordination centre and experimentation tools such as sandboxes. It guides regulators; it is not binding and the minister's foreword says a government resolution adopting it is still to be sought.

instruments.summary: Multi-year (2021-2026) national AI program, budgeted at about NIS 1 billion, coordinated through TELEM partners (MOST, Finance, Defense R&D directorate, Planning and Budgeting Committee, Innovation Authority, National Digital Agency, Foreign Affairs and Justice). It sets five objectives: AI infrastructure (research, talent, compute), AI in high-tech, safe AI in the public sector, Israel's international geo-technological position, and preparation of ministries for AI in their domains, with performance indicators. An English version is also published.

instruments.summary: National AI strategy formulated under Government Resolution 4255 ('Accelerating AI in Israel and Establishing Global Leadership'). Its two goals are making Israel a global AI power and turning that into prosperity and better daily life; it plans a National AI Institute with acceleration 'reactors', a national compute base, data and energy measures, 'enabling regulation' (removing barriers, regulatory experimentation) and a National Ethics Council to advise government and regulators on algorithmic transparency, fairness, privacy and human authority in decisions.

instruments.english_title: Privacy Protection Law, 5741-1981 (as amended by Amendment No. 13, 2024)
instruments.issuing_authority: Knesset (administered by the Privacy Protection Authority, Ministry of Justice)
instruments.publisher_name: Privacy Protection Authority (PPA), Ministry of Justice
instruments.current_status: In force. Source is the PPA's unofficial English translation 'Updated After Amendment 13'. Amendment 13 dates from the PPA's official guide to Amendment 13 (May 2025).
instruments.summary: Israel's general data protection law, which governs the collection and processing of personal data in databases, including for AI training and use. Amendment No. 13 (passed 5 August 2024, in force 14 August 2025) updated core definitions, required data protection officers in public bodies and many companies, replaced most database registration with notification and gave the Privacy Protection Authority inspection, administrative-fine and enforcement powers. The PPA relies on it for its AI guidance.

instruments.summary: Draft interpretive guideline setting out how the PPA will apply the Privacy Protection Law and its regulations, and its Amendment 13 enforcement powers, to databases that use AI. It covers lawful basis and informed consent across the AI lifecycle including training, disclosure that a person is interacting with AI, accountability and privacy impact assessment, AI-specific data-security risks, data-subject rights and the scraping of online personal data for training. Published for public comment; no final version found by 6 October 2026.

instruments.summary: Government guide for public bodies adopting AI, issued in the context of Government Resolution 3574 (4 December 2025) on data and AI in government. It sets responsible-use principles based on the OECD principles, AI governance roles (management, an AI governance lead, business owners, an optional AI governance forum), and a traffic-light risk process with green, yellow and red approval tracks plus a supervised 'blue' experimentation track. It includes a model organisational AI policy and rules for civil servants using AI tools, such as limits on entering data into external systems and verifying outputs. It does not override other procedures.

instruments.summary: Final report of the inter-ministerial team setting nine guiding principles for AI regulation in the supervised financial sector, among them flexible and adaptive regulation, alignment with international practice, removal of barriers, regulatory experimentation tools, regulation only where justified, a risk-based approach and consumer and social considerations. It sets policy lines on explainability, human involvement, disclosure, privacy, bias, cyber, fraud and competition, and on a financial-sector sandbox. It guides the financial regulators; it does not itself impose binding rules.

instruments.publisher_name: Bank of Israel – Banking Supervision Department
instruments.current_status: Published 21 August 2024 (Circular 06-2792); commencement 21 August 2025; existing material models within 6 months and others within 18 months of commencement.
instruments.summary: Banking directive requiring banking corporations and systemically important payment service providers to manage model risk through board and management oversight, model development and use controls and independent validation. It applies expressly to models that use or rely on AI, requiring banks to address AI-specific features such as explainability, ethics, data and accountability; an annex gives examples for AI models. Issued with Circular C-06-2792 on 21 August 2024; in force one year after publication, with transition periods for existing models.

instruments.current_status: Version dated January 2026 (Shevat 5786); replaces earlier ministry guidance.
instruments.summary: Ministry rules for using generative AI in schools: no student use in grades 1-3, the ministry's own bot from grade 4, teacher-controlled use in grades 5-6 and independent use of approved tools from grade 7. Use requires parental consent and prior training of staff and pupils, and must follow principles of privacy, non-discrimination, transparency, accountability and safety, with attention to pupil well-being.
